Proof of concept ·Opus 5.5 vision ·15 October 2026

Spill detection for the cleaning robot

A camera frame goes in, a yes/no verdict with a location comes out. No training data was collected and no model was trained. A general vision model reads each frame against a written description of what a floor spill is, and every answer it gives is stored as a label for the on-device model that comes next.

Pipeline

How a frame becomes a verdict

1 ·Sample

Pull frames from the camera

One or two frames per second is enough for a slow-moving robot. Near-identical frames are dropped so a parked robot does not keep paying to look at the same tile.

2 ·Ask

Vision model reads the frame

Claude Opus 5.5 receives the image and a written brief: what counts as a spill, what does not (reflections, shadows, dark tiles, wet-floor signs, liquid in cups). It must answer in a fixed JSON shape.

3 ·Act and keep

Verdict, box, reasoning

The robot gets a yes/no, a confidence, a liquid type and a box. The answer is also written to disk with the frame, so every run grows the training set for a small on-board model later.

What one answer looks like, for the first frame in the gallery below:

{
  "spill_detected": true,
  "confidence": 0.95,
  "spill_type": "water",
  "size": "large",
  "bbox": [
    0.0,
    0.47,
    1.0,
    0.25
  ],
  "debris_present": false,
  "floor_visible": true,
  "reasoning": "A large, irregularly shaped standing puddle of muddy water covers the concrete floor in front of the brick wall, with the wall clearly reflected in its surface. The distinct edges and reflection indicate real pooled liquid rather than a floor pattern or shadow."
}

Evaluation

Numbers behind the headline

100 frames drawn at random from the validation split of the public Spill_Detection dataset (Roboflow, CC BY 4.0). The dataset labels any visible liquid as "water", including coffee on a laptop or water on a sofa. Six of the 100 were like that. The model refused to call them floor spills, which is the behaviour we want, so they are reported separately rather than counted as misses.

All 100 frames, raw labelsFloor frames only (94)
Accuracy94%100%
Spills found55 of 6155 of 55
False alarms0 of 390 of 39
Non-floor liquids labelled "water"6, counted as missesexcluded

Caveat for the demo: the negatives in this public set are mostly unrelated photos (people, trolleys, bus stops). They prove the model does not hallucinate spills, but they are not the hard negatives a mall produces. Reflections on polished stone, dark tiles and shadows will be tested on our own robot-height footage next.

Model choice

Why Opus 5.5 and not the cheaper model

Claude Haiku 5.5 costs about a thirtieth as much. On the same 100 frames its headline score is slightly higher, but for the wrong reasons: it ignored the floor-only rule on three of the six mislabelled frames, and it missed the one genuinely hard floor spill in the set.

Claude Opus 5.5
Spill confidence 0.93

A tipped-over glass sits on a wood-grain floor, with a clear liquid puddle spreading from its rim. The puddle has distinct raised, reflective edges and darkens the wood beneath it.

Claude Haiku 5.5
Clear confidence 0.85

The frame shows a clear glass in the foreground and its reflections and refractions on a glossy, light-colored floor. The distorted shapes on the floor are reflections or shadows of the glass rather than liquid, and no puddle or wet patch is visible.

Claude Opus 5.5Claude Haiku 5.5
Floor-frame accuracy100%99%
Floor spills missed0 of 551 of 55
False alarms0 of 390 of 39
Followed the floor-only rule6 of 63 of 6
Cost, 100 frames$0.59$0.017
Mean latency3.2 s2.0 s

Recommendation: Opus 5.5 for the proof of concept and for labelling anything subtle. Haiku may later take the easy frames in bulk, with Opus re-checking anything it marks below 0.8 confidence.

Cost at scale

What this costs to run

ScenarioFramesEstimated cost
One robot, 1 frame/s, 8 h shift28,800$170 per shift
One robot, 1 frame every 5 s, 8 h shift5,760$34 per shift
Label 10,000 frames for training10,000$59 once

Per-frame cost measured in this run with prompt caching active. The cloud model is the proof-of-concept and labelling engine. The production robot runs a small on-device model trained on these labels, with no per-frame cost, and calls the cloud only for frames it is unsure about.

Next

Roadmap

In progress
Robot-height footage. Filming staged spills (water, oil, soy sauce) at 30 to 60 cm camera height on home floors, plus clean passes for hard negatives. Same pipeline, same report.
Next
Mall-floor hard negatives. Polished stone, reflections, dark tiles, wet-floor signs, shadows from trolleys. Measure the false-alarm rate where it actually matters.
Then
First robot run. Ten minutes of real robot camera video, driven past a few staged spills. Tune the brief on the errors.
Later
On-device model. Train a small detector from the accumulated labels and boxes so the robot runs offline at full frame rate, with the cloud model as a second opinion.
